narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in Bergamo, Italy, with records dating back to the early 16th century.
It was initially a peasant dance that gained popularity in instrumental music throughout the 17th century before falling out of fashion as a folk practice.
on_screen: Map: Italy · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It served as a form of rustic entertainment and was often associated with buffoonery.
It is famously depicted as a peasant dance in Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance was performed in a circular formation by couples.
Men moved forward while women moved backward until the melody shifted, at which point couples would embrace and turn before restarting the cycle.
Watch for Circular progression.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music was originally in 2/4 time, characterized by a lively, jumping rhythm and a repeating I–IV–V–I chord progression.
It was frequently played on the lute, keyboard, and strings.
Listen for the Lute, Keyboard, Strings.
The pulse is 2/4 (original), 6/8 (19th century).
Lively, jumping instrumental music based on a repeating harmonic cycle (I-IV-V-I), often featuring counterpoint in later baroque iterations.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Aria sopra 'la bergamasca' — Marco Uccellini; Antiche arie e danze per liuto (Suite #2) — Ottorino Respighi
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: I–IV–V–I chord progression

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Associated with rustic settings and the commedia dell'arte, the dance was performed by peasants and later adapted for theatrical and courtly instrumental settings.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key composers include Marco Uccellini, Salomone Rossi, Girolamo Frescobaldi, Samuel Scheidt, and in the 20th century, Ottorino Respighi.
In the 19th century, the term 'bergamasca' was applied to a different, lively 6/8 dance similar to the tarantella.
The dance shares structural similarities with the chaconne, passacaglia, and romanesca, often utilizing ostinato bass patterns.

scenes.title: Family tree
